ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Addiction Medicine Consultation — Calamity Jane — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: One-week review, seen the same day by addiction medicine: after withdrawal, a medicine for alcohol use disorder, the liver plan and recovery supports

text.paragraph: Severe alcohol use disorder in a 44-year-old woman without stable housing, starting outpatient withdrawal management today. Please confirm the diagnosis, review the withdrawal plan and advise on a medicine for alcohol use disorder, her liver, her mood and recovery support. [S]
Urgency: Within one week, on the same day as her one-week primary care visit. [S]

list.item: Do you agree with severe alcohol use disorder, and is outpatient withdrawal management safe for her?
Which medicine for alcohol use disorder do you advise, given her liver tests and that she moves between places?
How should we assess her liver after a FIB-4 of 3.93?
Should her depressive symptoms be treated now or reassessed after some weeks without alcohol?
What recovery support, harm reduction and attention to her housing and food do you suggest?

text.paragraph: Ms. Canary, a 44-year-old woman who does odd jobs and moves between towns, is seen at the request of Dr. Kessler one week after starting outpatient withdrawal management. She has drunk heavily for most of her adult life and has tried to stop many times on her own. Her last drink was a week ago. With gabapentin, thiamine and daily nurse checks, her withdrawal peaked at a CIWA-Ar of 10 on the second day and is now over. She wants to stop drinking altogether, does not want to be lectured, and would rather not take a pill every day if there is another way. She has a friend who supports her and has met the clinic's peer recovery specialist. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Calamity Jane was born Martha Canary about 1856, perhaps on May 1, near Princeton in Mercer County, Missouri, the eldest of six children of Robert and Charlotte Canary; the 1860 census lists her as born in 1856. Many popular accounts give 1852. [D]

Her family moved to the Montana gold camps about 1864; in December 1864 a Virginia City newspaper reported the Canary girls destitute. Her mother died at Blackfoot City, Montana Territory, in 1866 and her father in Utah in 1867, leaving her an orphan of about eleven with younger brothers and sisters. [D]

After her parents' deaths she made her way alone through the railroad construction camps and military posts of Wyoming, working as a dance-hall girl, waitress and laundress, and later at work usually done by men, such as driving ox teams as a bullwhacker and hauling wood. She often wore men's clothing, including buckskins. [D]

In 1875 she joined the Newton-Jenney expedition to the Black Hills without authorization, and by 1876 she was known as Calamity Jane; how she came by the name is uncertain, and the story that an army captain named her after she saved his life is unconfirmed. [D]
In June 1876 she traveled to Deadwood in a wagon train that included James Butler (Wild Bill) Hickok, who was murdered in Deadwood on August 2, 1876. [D]
Stories of a romance or marriage between her and Hickok are legend; her biographers find that they were acquaintances for a few weeks and that no evidence supports a love affair. [R]
During a smallpox epidemic in the Black Hills in 1878 she nursed sick people, and several contemporaries and memoirists remembered her as a nurse to the sick and a helper of people in need. [D]

Her 1896 autobiographical pamphlet, Life and Adventures of Calamity Jane, By Herself, written with a ghostwriter, describes exploits as an army scout and rider that historians regard as largely imaginary. [D]

Newspapers and contemporaries repeatedly reported her heavy drinking from the 1870s on; she was arrested for intoxication and disorderly conduct, and her principal biographer writes that every effort to end her drinking failed. Her drinking, wandering and lack of money left her poor even in settled periods. [D]
Historians describe her as an alcoholic; a diagnosis in present-day terms cannot be made from the historical record. [R]
She gave birth to a son in 1882 who died soon after birth, and to a daughter in 1887. [D]
In the mid-1880s, newspapers in Rawlins, Wyoming, reported that a man she lived with, and later married, beat her and stole from her. [D]

In the 1880s and 1890s she moved from town to town in Montana, Wyoming and the Dakotas, working in hotels and saloons and hauling wood, selling copies of her pamphlet and photographs, living at times on the help of acquaintances, and for a time staying in a pest house set aside for people with communicable diseases. [D]
In 1896 she toured the northern United States with the Kohl and Middleton dime museum show. [D]

In February 1901 she fell ill on a train journey from Livingston, Montana, and, having no money, was taken to the Gallatin County poor farm at Bozeman; she was discharged within days, and afterwards she angrily denied newspaper reports that she had been a county charge. [D]

code.displayName: Relevant Diagnostic Tests and/or Laboratory Data

list.item: Severe alcohol use disorder (F10.20). Nine DSM-5-TR criteria, including craving, failed attempts to cut down, use despite harm to her health and her work, tolerance and withdrawal: a severe disorder. Her long drinking began in a childhood of loss and poverty, and it is met here with treatment, not blame. [S]

Alcohol withdrawal (F10.230). With a PAWSS of 3, no past seizures or delirium, a support person and daily checks, ambulatory management was appropriate under the ASAM guideline, and gabapentin was a reasonable choice for mild withdrawal in a woman likely to be alone at times and with raised liver tests. Withdrawal is now complete. [S]

Medicine for alcohol use disorder (F10.20). Naltrexone is a first-line choice under the APA guideline and suits her goal of stopping. Her AST is under three times the upper limit and she has no signs of cirrhosis or hepatitis, so it can be used with liver tests rechecked. The monthly extended-release injection removes the need for a daily pill and suits a woman who moves between places. Acamprosate is the alternative if naltrexone cannot be used; disulfiram is not advised with her liver tests and without someone to supervise doses. She takes no opioids, and the urine test confirms it. [S]

Raised liver enzymes with a high FIB-4 (R74.01). An AST twice the ALT with a high GGT and macrocytosis fits alcohol-associated liver injury. A FIB-4 above 2.67 needs transient elastography; done after a few weeks without alcohol, it is less likely to be falsely raised by inflammation. Bilirubin, albumin, INR and platelets show no sign of liver failure. [S]

Depressive symptoms during heavy drinking (F32.A). Depressive symptoms during heavy drinking often improve within two to four weeks of stopping. With no suicidal thoughts and a safety plan in place, reassessment with the PHQ-9 at about four weeks is reasonable before deciding on an antidepressant. [S]

Recovery, harm reduction and social needs. Recovery is likelier with housing, food and someone to call. Peer support and a mutual-help group of her choice, including women-only options, help many women. Women develop liver damage after less drinking and fewer years than men, and alcohol raises breast cancer risk; she should hear this plainly. A plan for a return to drinking keeps her safe and in care. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Kessler's intake note and safety assessment; the nurse's daily CIWA-Ar scores (10 at most, 2 today). AUDIT 31, PEth 820 ng/mL, PHQ-9 14, GAD-7 11 and PC-PTSD-5 2 at intake. Intake laboratory results: AST 96, ALT 44 and GGT 240 U/L, albumin 3.4 g/dL, bilirubin 1.1 mg/dL, INR 1.0, platelets 162, MCV 103 fL; FIB-4 3.93. Today potassium 3.9 mmol/L and magnesium 1.8 mg/dL after replacement. HIV and hepatitis C negative; hepatitis B not infected and not immune; urine drug test negative for opioids, fentanyl and other drugs; pregnancy test negative. [S]

list.item: Start naltrexone 50 mg daily now; change to extended-release naltrexone 380 mg intramuscularly every four weeks if daily tablets are hard to keep. [S]
Recheck liver enzymes at about four weeks and then periodically; stop naltrexone for symptoms of hepatitis. [S]
Give her a wallet card stating that naltrexone blocks opioids; treat pain with non-opioid medicines. [S]
Transient elastography at about four weeks without alcohol, and again after several months; hepatitis A and B vaccination. [S]
PHQ-9 and GAD-7 at four weeks; an antidepressant only if symptoms persist after a month or more without alcohol. [S]
PEth at about four weeks and every one to two months, explained as part of care. [S]
Weekly peer recovery contact and a mutual-help group of her choice (Alcoholics Anonymous, SMART Recovery or Women for Sobriety). [S]
A written plan for a return to drinking: call the peer specialist or the clinic, eat, do not drink alone or drive, keep taking naltrexone, and come back without shame. [S]
Continue thiamine 100 mg and folic acid 1 mg daily. [S]
Medicaid, SNAP, a food bank and the local housing program through the community health worker. [S]
Discussed with Dr. Kessler, who saw her the same day. The options were explained to Ms. Canary in plain words; she chose to start naltrexone tablets and to consider the monthly injection. [S]

Follow-up: Dr. Kessler continues prescribing and the monthly reviews; addiction medicine will see her again if she returns to drinking for more than a few days, cannot use naltrexone, or wants to discuss another medicine. [S]
